citation_policy: Cite at most two outside sources per post. More looks like padding.
Every outside link must be one of the URLs in this registry. Never invent, guess, or reconstruct a government URL.
Link with descriptive anchor text naming the publisher, for example 'the California Secretary of State apostille FAQ'. Never use 'click here' or a bare URL.
Cite a source only for the subject listed in its authoritative_for field. Do not use a notary handbook link to support a claim about facility policy or fees.
claims_that_require_a_cited_source: Any fee, cost, or dollar amount
Any processing time, turnaround, or deadline
Any statement about what the law requires or prohibits
Any statement about which agency handles a document type
Any statement about whether a country accepts an apostille
rules.if_no_source_supports_the_claim: Omit the claim entirely. Do not soften it, do not hedge it, and do not substitute a general statement. An unsourced specific is the single biggest factual risk in this content.
verified_factual_corrections: The federal authentication step is the U.S. Department of STATE, Office of Authentications. It is NOT the Department of Justice. Neither State Department page nor USA.gov mentions any DOJ role in authenticating documents for use abroad. The California Department of Justice appears elsewhere in our content for Live Scan fingerprint background checks, which is a separate and unrelated process; do not let the two cross over.

California issues a single apostille regardless of destination country, confirmed by direct quote from the CA SOS apostille FAQ. Some other states issue a distinct non-Hague certification instead, so guidance written for another state does not transfer to California.

At the FEDERAL level the apostille versus authentication-certificate distinction does exist: the U.S. Department of State issues an apostille for Hague member countries and an authentication certificate for non-member countries.

NOT SOURCEABLE from a U.S. federal page: the final embassy or consulate legalization step for a non-member country. Neither the State Department Office of Authentications page nor USA.gov states it. The authority for that final step is the destination country's own consulate, because requirements vary by country. Frame it that way and link the consulate, rather than asserting a generic final step as if a U.S. agency published it.
never_do: Never state or imply legal advice, or which document a reader should use. That is the unauthorized practice of law and is outside a notary's authority.

Do not use 'authentication' as a loose synonym for the California apostille, which is the old error we are avoiding. But DO use 'authentication certificate' in its correct technical sense: the specific certificate the U.S. Department of State issues for non-Hague destinations. The banned usage is calling a CA SOS apostille an authentication; the correct usage is the federal non-member certificate.
Never claim a specific fee or turnaround for a government agency.
Never cite a commercial competitor, an apostille agency, or an SEO blog as a source.

Do not name the Department of Justice as the agency that AUTHENTICATES documents for use abroad. DOJ and the FBI issue certain federal documents; the U.S. Department of State authenticates them. Name the correct role for each.

document_routing._rule: Determine the issuing authority FIRST. It decides the entire path. Getting this wrong is the most damaging factual error possible in apostille content, because it sends a reader to the wrong agency and wastes weeks.

federal_documents.path: Straight to the U.S. Department of State, Office of Authentications. NO state step. California SOS has no role and cannot apostille these.
federal_documents.then_if_non_hague: State Department issues an authentication certificate instead of an apostille, then the destination country's consulate legalizes it.

critical_requirements: A federal document MUST NOT be notarized. Notarizing it can invalidate the submission. This is counterintuitive and worth stating plainly on the FBI background check page.
Original or certified copy only, with original seals and signatures, a date of issuance, agency letterhead, and a legible signature with printed name and title.
If a translation is needed, the TRANSLATION is notarized, but the original federal document is still not notarized.
federal_documents.terminology_nuance: The DOJ and FBI ISSUE these documents. The U.S. Department of State AUTHENTICATES them. Both agencies are legitimately part of the story, so be precise about which role each plays rather than treating DOJ as the authenticating body.

federal_detention_facilities._why_this_matters: Federal detention is a completely different legal regime from a county jail. LASD rules and California notary practice do not transfer to MDC Los Angeles, Terminal Island, or ICE facilities. Never reuse county jail language for a federal facility.
federal_detention_facilities.who_can_already_do_it_inside: Under 18 U.S.C. 4004 the warden, associate warden, chief clerk, and record clerk may administer oaths and take acknowledgments for inmates, and may not charge a fee. BOP policy assigns witnessing to institution Case Managers.
federal_detention_facilities.most_federal_filings_need_no_notary: BOP policy states that for documents filed in federal courts or with federal agencies, staff need not administer oaths or witness signatures unless the court or agency directs it, because 28 U.S.C. 1746 lets the inmate sign an unsworn declaration under penalty of perjury instead.
federal_detention_facilities.where_an_outside_notary_still_matters: BOP policy itself says documents for submission to STATE courts and STATE agencies may require a sworn declaration. A California deed, DMV title transfer, statutory power of attorney, or state court filing signed by a federal inmate is the real use case, because the 18 U.S.C. 4004 authority is a federal witnessing power and not a California notarial act.
federal_detention_facilities.access_reality: The MDC Los Angeles handbook authorizes legal visits for attorneys with valid Bar Association cards and does not list notaries as authorized legal visitors. 28 CFR 543.11 likewise contemplates only an authorized attorney visit from a retained attorney. Do not imply walk-in or scheduled notary access to a federal facility the way we describe county jails. Access is arranged through the inmate's attorney or the facility, at the facility's discretion.
federal_detention_facilities.access_mechanism: A notary does not enter a federal facility as a notary. They enter as the REPRESENTATIVE OF A LICENSED ATTORNEY using BOP form BP-A0243, accompanied in practice by a letter on the attorney's letterhead authorizing the visit. The form is a full background questionnaire: date of birth, five years of address history, five years of employment history, education from grade 10 forward, criminal and confinement history, and any prior BOP visit denials. The sponsoring attorney must certify bar membership, that they employ or supervise the representative, and must accept personal and professional responsibility for all acts of that representative inside the institution.
federal_detention_facilities.business_implication: Because a sponsoring attorney is structurally REQUIRED, federal facility work is inherently a B2B referral channel and cannot be sold directly to a family the way county jail work can. Content about federal facilities should be written for attorneys and their staff, not for families, because the attorney is the only party who can authorize entry. This is the strongest business-partner angle in the entire content plan.
federal_detention_facilities.do_not_publish: Never reproduce a filled BP-A0243 in public content. A completed form contains the representative's date of birth and home address, and names a specific inmate. Use only the blank official form and describe the fields in general terms.
federal_detention_facilities.content_guidance: Write this as an honest explainer that saves the reader a wasted trip: for most federal paperwork they need no notary at all, and the facility can handle oaths for free. Then explain the narrow state-document case. That honesty is the differentiator, because competitors advertise federal jail notary service without addressing any of this.

notary_federal_detention.authoritative_for: BOP policy on inmate oaths, witnessing, and unsworn declarations
notary_federal_detention.notes: Controlling source for federal facilities. Key quotes: 'Inmates and staff will be able to make oaths and affirmations and have them witnessed by institution Case Managers, as authorized by 18 U.S.C. 4004.' And: 'Other than for the exceptions cited above, staff need not administer oaths and witness inmate signatures on any documents to be filed in Federal courts or with Federal agencies, unless directly instructed to do so by the Court or agency.' And the opening for outside notaries: 'documents for submission to state courts and state agencies may require a sworn declaration.'

notary_federal_detention.publisher: U.S. House, Office of the Law Revision Counsel
notary_federal_detention.authoritative_for: 18 U.S.C. 4004, the in-house federal authority to administer oaths and take acknowledgments
notary_federal_detention.notes: Exact text: wardens, associate wardens, chief clerks, and record clerks of Federal penal or correctional institutions 'may administer oaths to and take acknowledgments of officers, employees, and inmates of such institutions, but shall not demand or accept any fee or compensation therefor.' Note the no-fee clause: this is a free in-house service, so a federal facility has no need to bring in a paid notary for federal filings.

notary_federal_detention.publisher: U.S. House, Office of the Law Revision Counsel
notary_federal_detention.authoritative_for: 28 U.S.C. 1746, unsworn declaration under penalty of perjury
notary_federal_detention.notes: Statutory language a reader can actually use: 'I declare (or certify, verify, or state) under penalty of perjury under the laws of the United States of America that the foregoing is true and correct. Executed on (date).' Excludes depositions, oaths of office, and oaths required before an official other than a notary public.

The regulation contemplates only 'an authorized attorney visit from a retained attorney' and never identifies notaries as authorized visitors.

notary_federal_detention.authoritative_for: Form BP-A0243, the actual mechanism by which a non-attorney enters a federal facility
notary_federal_detention.notes: Official title: 'Application to Enter Institution as the Representative of a Licensed Attorney or to Correspond with a Federal Prisoner as the Representative of a Licensed Attorney.' Prescribed by P1315. Three parts: a questionnaire, an applicant certification, and a sponsoring attorney statement. The questionnaire requires date of birth, five years of addresses, five years of employers, education from grade 10 forward, criminal history, confinement history, and prior BOP visit denials. The sponsoring attorney must certify bar membership, that the attorney employs or supervises the representative, and must 'accept personal and professional responsibility for all acts of my representative which affect the institution, its inmates or staff.' This is the form our own operator actually submits, plus a letter on the attorney's letterhead.

consular_legalization.authoritative_for: That California issues ONE apostille regardless of destination country
consular_legalization.notes: Direct quote: 'The California Secretary of State issues a single Apostille for documents to be used outside of the United States, regardless of the country of destination.' California does not issue a separate non-Hague certification the way some other states do. Note this page is SILENT on what to do next for a non-member country.

consular_legalization.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of Authentications
consular_legalization.authoritative_for: The federal step for non-Hague destinations, and Form DS-4194
consular_legalization.notes: This office issues BOTH apostilles (Hague member countries) and authentication certificates (non-member countries). It is the U.S. Department of State, NOT the Department of Justice. Sourced specifics: Form DS-4194; mail requests processed within five weeks; walk-in is one request per day capped at 15 documents and processed in seven business days; same-day appointments exist only for the death, dying, or life-threatening illness of an immediate family member abroad.
